title: Question 1.1 (Question 10 in Fitzpatrick et al.)
statement_text: Is $z(G \square H) \leq z(G) + z(H)$ for all graphs $G$ and $H$?
context_text: The zombie number $z(G)$ is the minimum number of zombies needed to capture the survivor in the deterministic Zombies and Survivors game on $G$. This question asks whether the zombie number of the Cartesian product of two graphs is bounded by the sum of their individual zombie numbers.
paper_contribution: Proves the answer is yes: Theorem 1.3 establishes $z(G \square H) \leq z(G) + z(H)$ for all graphs $G$ and $H$, fully answering the question in the affirmative.
notes: PDF source uses '6' to denote ≤; interpreted accordingly.

title: Question 1.2 (Question 19 in Fitzpatrick et al.)
statement_text: Over all graphs $G$, how large can the ratio $\frac{z(G)}{c(G)}$ be?
context_text: This question compares the zombie number $z(G)$ to the cop number $c(G)$, asking whether zombies can require arbitrarily many more players than cops to capture the survivor. The paper shows this ratio is unbounded.
paper_contribution: Shows via Theorem 1.4 that the ratio $z(G)/c(G)$ can be arbitrarily large, constructing a family of cactus graphs $G_k$ (unions of odd cycles sharing a vertex) with $c(G_k) = 2$ and $z(G_k) > k$ for every integer $k$.

title: Question 4.1
statement_text: For every graph $G$, and for a graph $G'$ obtained from $G$ by successively adding vertices of degree 1, does it always hold that $z(G') = z(G)$?
context_text: Graphs are connected. In the game of (deterministic) Zombies and Survivors, a variant of Cops and Robber, zombies play the role of cops and a single survivor the role of the robber; in each round every zombie must move along some shortest path (geodesic) towards the survivor (when several geodesics exist, the zombies may choose which one), and the zombies win if one of them moves onto the survivor's vertex. The zombie number $z(G)$ is the minimum number of zombies that can be placed in $G$ so as to ensure that the survivor is eventually captured, and the cop number $c(G)$ is the analogous minimum for cops (which can move freely to a neighbour or stay); clearly $c(G)\le z(G)$. The paper proves $z(G\,\square\,H)\le z(G)+z(H)$ for the Cartesian product, answering a question of Fitzpatrick et al., and gives graphs with cop number 2 and arbitrarily large zombie number. The authors interpret the question as asking whether zombies could gain an advantage by waiting individually for some pre-announced time at the start of the game before following the standard rules. The authors pose it, together with a question on subdivisions, as touching on whether, when the survivor plays to survive as long as possible, all $z(G)$ zombies are close to it at the time of capture.

title: Question 4.2
statement_text: For any graph $G$, is there an integer $k$ such that, for $G'_k$ the graph obtained from $G$ by subdividing all edges $k$ times then adding the original edges, $z(G'_k) \geq z(G) + 1$?
context_text: Graphs are connected. In the game of (deterministic) Zombies and Survivors, a variant of Cops and Robber, zombies play the role of cops and a single survivor the role of the robber; in each round every zombie must move along some shortest path (geodesic) towards the survivor (when several geodesics exist, the zombies may choose which one), and the zombies win if one of them moves onto the survivor's vertex. The zombie number $z(G)$ is the minimum number of zombies that can be placed in $G$ so as to ensure that the survivor is eventually captured, and the cop number $c(G)$ is the analogous minimum for cops (which can move freely to a neighbour or stay); clearly $c(G)\le z(G)$. The paper proves $z(G\,\square\,H)\le z(G)+z(H)$ for the Cartesian product, answering a question of Fitzpatrick et al., and gives graphs with cop number 2 and arbitrarily large zombie number. In $G'_k$ each edge $uv$ of $G$ is kept and also replaced by a path from $u$ to $v$ with $k$ new internal vertices, so $G$ is an isometric subgraph of $G'_k$ and the original vertices keep their distances. The authors remark that, as far as they can tell, $k=5$ might be a valid answer for every graph $G$.
notes: PDF source — the inequality $z(G'_k) > z(G) + 1$ may be garbled; it could be $z(G'_k) \geq z(G) + 1$ (a strict increase of at least 1). The follow-up remark 'it could be that 5 is a valid answer to Question 4.2 in any graph' suggests the question may additionally seek a universal constant $k$.
